item.title: Claude Code Game Restrictions Target Clones, But Developers Say Legitimate Projects Are Being Blocked
item.description:
Anthropic has introduced new Claude Code game restrictions designed to prevent its AI coding assistant from recreating existing video games. However, the change is already generating controversy, with some developers reporting that the restrictions are also interfering with their own projects .

As first reported by Game Developer , the new instruction was discovered by X user Chasm , who claims it was introduced around October 27 through a server-delivered configuration identified as tengu_heron_brook .

The instruction explicitly tells Claude Code not to recreate specific existing games, even when presented under different names :

"Do not build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."

More importantly, this doesn't represent a blanket prohibition on AI-assisted game development. Anthropic specifically allows the creation of original games, projects inspired by existing genres, and games built using users' own designs and assets.

Anthropic's Addy Osmani subsequently confirmed the change , explaining that two sentences had been added to Claude Code's prompt for Opus 5.5 to discourage intellectual property infringement, which already violates the company's usage policy.

Osmani also acknowledged the potential for unintended consequences, stating that Anthropic would continue refining the restrictions and encouraging developers whose own projects were incorrectly rejected to report their experiences.

Unfortunately, such complaints have already emerged. In a GitHub issue filed on October 30 , a developer operating Conflict Simulations LLC reported that Claude Code had started refusing to work on personalized digital board-wargame modules commissioned by paying customers.

According to the developer, these projects use original code and customer-supplied materials, with the resulting modules intended exclusively for customers who own the corresponding physical games. However, the developer clarified that the work isn't officially licensed by the games' publishers.

Interestingly, the developer claims the refusals began only after asking Claude to evaluate whether the new restrictions applied to the existing project.

Meanwhile, Tom's Hardware reports additional complaints involving reverse-engineering workflows, although a direct connection to the game-specific instruction hasn't been conclusively established.

These developments are particularly relevant to the PC modding community, where AI-assisted coding tools have increasingly been used for reverse engineering, optimization, and game preservation.

For instance, we recently covered an Oblivion Remastered performance mod developed with Claude AI, which reportedly improved average frame rates by over 40% while substantially reducing traversal stuttering .

The new Claude Code game restrictions don't explicitly prohibit modding or optimizing existing games , but the reported refusals raise questions about how reliably the tool can distinguish unauthorized recreations from other development activities.

Ultimately, Anthropic faces the challenge of protecting developers' intellectual property without unnecessarily restricting legitimate uses of its increasingly capable AI coding tools.

News Sources: Chasm (X) , Game Developer , and Tom's Hardware

item.title: Buyer Snags Core i9-9900K Gaming PC With An RTX 2070 And 32GB RAM For $250 Over BSODs Occurring When Running Arc Raiders; Updating Drivers Fixed The Problem
item.description:
Intel’s Core i9-9900K and RTX 2070 is still a solid pairing in 2026 if you want to play the newest titles at lowered settings or want to get some content creator workloads tackled, and for $250, it’s a super steal of a deal. One buyer successfully managed to grab this configuration, which also came with 32GB of DDR4, because the original owner was experiencing BSODs, but only when playing Arc Raiders. Turns out that all it took was a driver update to eliminate the issue.

Considering that 32GB of DDR4 RAM costs nearly $200, the buyer’s luck was on his side

Instead of treating the BSODs as a red flag, Redditor “u/lovelybitxhh” took matters into his own hands, updated the drivers, and says the problem hasn’t returned. He also mentions that all temperatures are fine, and sums up the deal by calling it “not an insane build but definitely an insane price.” The photos show a white case, which appears to be an NZXT model, with an ASRock Z390 Phantom Gaming motherboard inside.

The CPU is cooled by what looks like a liquid cooler, with the RTX 2070 graphics card sitting in the PCIe slot with braided power cables. The hardware dates back to 2018, when both the Core i9-9900K and the RTX 2070 launched. The CPU’s eight cores and sixteen threads still handle modern games reasonably well, while the RTX 2070 remains a workable card for 1080p gaming. Sadly, the Redditor didn’t include any benchmarks or framerate numbers to show how this configuration is holding up in 2026.

However, the post has been rather ambiguous about the driver updating part. The Redditor doesn’t clarify if he’s referring to the graphics driver, chipset drivers, or something else, and it’s unclear how long the system has been tested since. Based on our experience, outdated chipset drivers and multiple instances of display drivers often result in incessant BSODs, and if the PC user isn’t well-versed with various error codes or checking Windows features like Reliability Monitor or Event Viewer, he or she may conclude that these crashes are hardware-related.

Even so, the deal highlights how much value can sit in the used market when sellers assume a machine is faulty. A complete system with a high-end CPU of its era, a dedicated GPU, and 32GB DDR4 RAM for $250 is a price few new or refurbished options can match, and a simple software update appears to have been all it took to fix it. As with any marketplace purchase, though, buyers are taking a risk, and not every “blue screening” listing will turn out to be a driver issue.

item.title: OpenAI Teases GPT-6.1 Astra Amid Relentless Hype Around The Mysterious GPT-6.2 Betelgeuse Model, As Another Evidence Surfaces Showing Kimi K3.1 Pro And GLM-5.3 As Products Of Distillation
item.description:
OpenAI has done something different recently: offered banked resets that suggest it wants you to save your token splurge on a new model, likely GPT-6.1 Astra. Meanwhile, AI enthusiasts continue to speculate on the characteristics of the unreleased GPT-6.2 Betelgeuse model that has recently surfaced in online leaks.

At the other end of the spectrum, a personality test for Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro and Z.ai's GLM-5.3 has revealed uncanny similarities with the GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Claude 5 series, respectively, which suggests that both of these models are likely a product of distillation.

GPT-6.2 Betelgeuse has now been spotted within OpenAI's internal model tracker, as GPT-6.1 Astra likely lands next week

We noted a few weeks back that OpenAI has apparently finished pre-training its next base model, known internally as Bel , with over 10 trillion parameters under its belt. Now, GPT-6.2 Betelgeuse has surfaced within OpenAI's internal model tracker . Do note that Bel is likely to serve as the base model for Betelgeuse.

Meanwhile, OpenAI has begun hinting at an imminent launch, with GPT-6.1 Astra billed as the most likely release candidate . In what adds additional heft to this hypothesis, OpenAI has just announced token limit resets on a " banked " basis, which indicates that it wants its customers to really splurge on the next Astra-class model.

Of course, while America's two leading AI labs - OpenAI and Anthropic - are currently operating within a fairly healthy micro environment, with one model release after another, their macro environment is anything but.

As an illustration, consider the fact that OpenAI has so far managed to raise less than half of its targeted $30 billion haul in its most recent funding round, receiving firm commitments for just $11 billion . The AI lab is now reportedly seeking to raise just $20 billion at a valuation of $1.25 trillion .

Meanwhile, over at Anthropic, the Financial Times recently reported that it would likely command a 'junk' debt rating once it IPOs in November, which would be a serious limitation, especially given the fact that it has unfunded compute commitments worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

Another evidence points to the distilled nature of Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro and Z.ai's GLM-5.3

Meanwhile, Artificial Analysis' Personality Indexes have disclosed a fascinating insight into Kimi K3.1 Pro and GLM-5.3, showing an uncanny similarity with GPT-6 Astra in the case of the former and with Anthropic's Claude 5 series in the case of the latter.

These radar charts from Artificial Analysis’s AA-PersonalityBench suggest distillation, or at the very least, heavy stylistic influence via synthetic data.

Of course, surface personality similarity can also arise from convergent post-training - shared preferences for "helpful," expressive, low-slop writing; similar preference data; or deliberate style matching - without full distillation.

Interestingly, DeepSeek's V4.1-Flash-1017 shows no such affinity, which only gels with other ancillary evidence that suggests DeepSeek's models are largely the result of its own efforts.

item.title: China’s Iluvatar CoreX Claims Its Tiangai 300 GPU Beats NVIDIA’s H200 In Its Own Live Demo, But The Only Outside Test Shows Just A 5% Lead
item.description:
Chinese chipmaker Iluvatar CoreX says its new Tiangai 300 GPU can match, and in some cases beat, NVIDIA’s H200 in real-world AI workloads, in the latest sign that domestic players are trying to narrow the gap with the U.S. giant. The newest claims come from a live demonstration for mainland Chinese media that happened on a Wednesday.

Tiangai 300 As A NVIDIA H200 Rival Using Its Own Benchmarks, While Third-Party Testing Shows A Slim Advantage

During the demonstration, the Shanghai-based firm ran text-to-image and text-to-video generation using frontier models such as Z.ai’s GLM-5.3. In one text-to-image test, the Tiangai 300 completed every task and managed 0.101 images per second, compared with an 87.5 percent completion rate and 0.086 images per second for NVIDIA’s H200. However, the Chinese chip did take 0.64 seconds longer to complete the task

It’s worth noting that Iluvatar CoreX’s claims are supported by a third-party test from state-backed Shanghai INESA, which found the Tiangai 300, unveiled in July, delivered 1.05 times the H200’s throughput under typical deployment conditions. Separate reporting from Wallstreetcn says the chip beat the H200 by 15 percent in mixture-of-experts (MoE) throughput and cut first-token latency by up to 30 percent in long-text processing.

For training, the GPU reportedly delivered 1.33 times the effective throughput of the older H100 when fine-tuning Alibaba’s Qwen3-32B. The H200 is the most advanced NVIDIA AI GPU that’s approved for export to China under current U.S. rules. The country has also discouraged domestic firms from purchasing foreign chips, giving rise to local rivals such as Biren, MetaX, Enflame, and Moore Threads, alongside Iluvatar CoreX.

Despite this rise, it’s not like Chinese companies are forgoing the purchase of NVIDIA GPUs entirely. After all, the CUDA software stack is a massive selling point for these firms, which is why even after U.S. export controls have barred the export of advanced AI GPUs like B300 , a security firm discovered 32 of these units operating inside China Telecom , likely deployed through smuggling.

Chinese technology behemoths like ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have also preferred the RTX PRO 5500 over Huawei’s Ascend 950PR thanks to superior inference capabilities, suggesting that NVIDIA will continue to have a major presence in the region, despite chips like Tiangai 300 gaining traction. Speaking of Tiangai 300, it’s worth mentioning that the benchmark results largely come from a company-run demo that was shown to friendly media.

The only outside figure, from INESA, is a 5 percent edge, which is hardly a decisive lead, and the training comparison is against the H100, not the H200. Iluvatar CoreX also remains small, sporting a measly 0.3 percent of China’s domestic general-purpose GPU market in 2024. Still, the Chinese firm appears determined in its mission, as not only did it get listed in Hong Kong earlier this year, but it also outlined a roadmap in January aiming to leapfrog NVIDIA’s Rubin platform within two years.

item.title: New NVIDIA UEFI GPU Unlocker Brings Up To 75% Higher AI Compute Performance To RTX 20, 30 & 40 Series GPUs On Windows
item.description:
A new open-source tool called NV UEFI Unlocker promises to unleash previously restricted Tensor Core compute performance on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 20, 30, and 40 Series GPUs, bringing functionality previously associated primarily with Linux-based modifications to Windows users.

Developed by GitHub user physicsdolphin, the NV UEFI Unlocker project uses a UEFI-based approach to modify GPU behavior before NVIDIA's graphics driver initializes . Unlike traditional firmware modifications, it doesn't require permanently flashing the GPU's VBIOS or patching NVIDIA's drivers . The unlock is temporary and disappears after a complete power-off.

As we previously reported on Wccftech , the original GPU Unlock project developed by Zagitta demonstrated that GeForce RTX 30 Series GPUs could achieve nearly twice their normal Tensor Core throughput in certain FP16/BF16 compute workloads. Real-world AI image-generation benchmarks also showed improvements approaching 60%, although the original implementation relied on a Linux kernel module. An experimental, hardware-specific Windows implementation had also emerged at the time.

NV UEFI Unlocker expands the accessibility of these modifications by supporting Windows, Linux, and other UEFI-bootable operating systems , while extending compatibility across three NVIDIA GPU generations. According to its official compatibility matrix , RTX 20, 30, and 40 Series GPUs are supported, although certain models still encounter issues. GTX 16 Series support remains experimental, while RTX 50 Series GPUs are unsupported.

Early benchmark results are promising. An RTX 2070 reportedly improved from 36 TFLOPS to approximately 60–63 TFLOPS in FP32-accumulation matrix multiplication, representing a 67–75% increase. Meanwhile, an RTX 4060 Laptop GPU demonstrated a 65% improvement in FP16 compute throughput , climbing from 29.89 to 49.33 TFLOPS. These gains have also attracted attention in a Reddit discussion on r/overclocking.

These findings complement Wccftech's previous coverage of RTX 30 and 40 Series compute unlocking , which highlighted substantial improvements in synthetic Tensor Core benchmarks and certain AI inference workloads.

The installation process, detailed in the project's official documentation, involves preparing a bootable USB drive containing the UEFI application and required firmware components. Users boot from the USB drive, allowing the tool to execute its modifications before automatically handing control back to the operating system. Secure Boot must either be disabled or configured to trust the EFI application , while RTX 20 Series users must first enable the required GSP firmware mode.

However, the project remains experimental, and successful unlocking isn't guaranteed across every GPU or system configuration. Higher theoretical compute throughput also doesn't necessarily translate into equivalent real-world gains, which depend heavily on workload characteristics, memory bandwidth, and power limitations.

There is also currently no convincing evidence that these modifications improve gaming performance or DLSS execution times.

Nevertheless, NV UEFI Unlocker represents another promising development for owners of older NVIDIA GPUs, especially those interested in extracting additional AI compute performance from their existing hardware without permanent modifications.

News Source: r/overclocking subreddit

item.title: Star Wars Jedi 3 Is Far Into Development and Could Be Revealed Soon, Jason Schreier Says, as Respawn Prepares Cal Kestis’ Final Chapter
item.description:
Bloomberg's Jason Schreier has confirmed that Respawn Entertainment is far into the development of Star Wars Jedi 3 , and the game's unveiling may come soon enough.

The questions were asked following his reveal that BioWare was shutdown and its Mass Effect game canceled because publisher Electronic Arts preferred to fund Star Wars Battlefront 3 instead . However, Jedi 3 was safe from this discussion precisely because it's nearly done.

The confirmation that the game was in development came directly from EA. When the previous installment, 2023's Jedi Survivor , launched on PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in September 2024, Laura Miele (president of EA Entertainment) said :

Respawn is working hard to bring the final chapter of this thrilling story to players.

In June, Insider Gaming's Tom Henderson claimed to have heard that the game would feature an older Cal Kestis , imply a possible time jump from Jedi Survivor.

Schreier's statement seems to confirm a previous leak from Star Wars insider FivesWalker, who mentioned that Star Wars Jedi 3 would be possibly announced this year (maybe at Geoff Keighley's The Game Awards, slated for December 10) and released sometime next year.

For PC players, hopefully the third installment will also deliver a much stronger technical showing . Jedi Survivor's launch was infamously marred by shader compilation and traversal stuttering , and significant problems persisted even after its ninth patch , more than 500 days after the original release. Whatever new locations, Force abilities, or combat options Respawn introduces for the new game, a smoother experience should be high on the studio's to-do list.

There is also an important distinction between a game being far into development and having a confirmed release window. Schreier’s comments are encouraging, but they do not turn the rumored 2027 launch or a possible appearance at The Game Awards into official announcements. For now, the prospect of an imminent reveal gives Star Wars Jedi fans something tangible to look forward to after years of waiting. The next trailer will have the considerable task of showing how Respawn intends to bring Cal Kestis’ trilogy to a satisfying conclusion .

item.title: Sam Altman Calls PC RAM A “Quite Terrible” Use Of Limited DRAM Supply, Argues Cloud Data Centers Are More Efficient
item.description:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes that having large amounts of RAM installed in personal computers is an inefficient use of the world's increasingly limited DRAM supply, arguing that cloud data centers can make better use of these resources. His comments come at a particularly controversial time, as the AI industry's enormous demand for memory continues to drive consumer hardware prices through the roof.

During a recent Cheeky Pint podcast interview with Stripe co-founder John Collison, Altman discussed the ongoing compute and memory shortages, including the growing interest in running open-source AI models locally rather than relying on cloud infrastructure.

According to Altman, some people believe that the availability of capable local AI models could significantly reduce the need for data centers. However, he disagrees with this assessment, pointing to the relatively low utilization of memory installed in personal computers.

"It's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer."

Altman estimated that such memory might be used only around 5% of the time , although he provided no supporting data for that figure. Instead, he argued that maximizing memory utilization through shared cloud infrastructure would make more sense in the current supply-constrained environment.

His remarks are particularly noteworthy given the unprecedented memory shortage currently affecting the consumer PC market , with AI infrastructure investments absorbing substantial manufacturing capacity.

As Wccftech recently reported , Samsung expects memory shortages to worsen in 2027, with supply constraints potentially continuing into 2028. The South Korean manufacturer has already sold out its 2027 HBM supply and secured long-term agreements covering approximately 60–70% of its production capacity.

Meanwhile, DDR5 memory prices in Japan have increased by as much as 761% for certain high-capacity kits over the past year. We also recently highlighted how a 32GB DDR5-7600 kit purchased for just $110 in 2024 is now advertised for more than $1,500, although substantially cheaper alternatives remain available.

Interestingly, Altman also acknowledged that the market has struggled to respond to the shortage, suggesting that memory manufacturers remain reluctant to invest aggressively in new production capacity following previous boom-and-bust cycles.

While his argument about resource utilization has some economic merit , local computing offers advantages that centralized cloud infrastructure cannot necessarily replicate, including offline operation, greater control over personal data, and independence from external services .

It's also worth emphasizing that Altman was discussing the efficiency of local AI inference rather than explicitly suggesting that consumers should stop purchasing RAM. Nevertheless, his comments are unlikely to sit well with PC enthusiasts already facing historically high memory prices, especially when the AI industry's enormous infrastructure requirements are among the primary contributors to the ongoing shortage.

item.title: Microsoft Veteran Engineer Explains Windows 11 Task Manager Lag Under Heavy CPU Load, Saying It’s “Hard To Fix A Runaway System From Within That Same System”
item.description:
Has your Task Manager frozen in Windows 11 when you’re running an extremely taxing program? If yes, you’re not the first and you certainly won’t be the last. Microsoft’s veteran software engineer Raymond Chen has addressed a frustration many users are quite familiar with, especially when a game, a browser with too many tabs, or a heavy app pushes a PC to its limits. As for a potential change, it appears as if things will remain as they are.

When Windows 11 runs out of CPU time, Chen says that every process suffers, including the Task Manager

On Microsoft’s Dev Blogs website, Windows Latest noticed Chen’s explanation, which also states that running Task Manager at high priority might sound simple and easy, but that’s not the case. Like this Windows 11 add-on, any program running at high priority will eventually hit a shared resource it has to wait for, and at that point it is stuck. He compares it to a priority checkout pass that gets you to the front of the line, though you still wait if the person at the cash register has a cart overflowing with groceries.

Fortunately, Windows 11 has a safeguard for one version of this problem. When code protecting a resource is built to avoid priority inversion, the waiting thread’s priority is passed on to the thread that owns the resource. Chen notes that this doesn’t help if the owning thread is busy with something slow, such as accessing a file over the network. UI code is especially vulnerable, since it eventually has to call into the UI system, where it competes with every other UI thread on the machine.

The app in focus is already receiving Windows’ preferential treatment, so Task Manager’s performance is about as good as you’re going to get it right now. However, that preference can only go so far, especially if the processing threads end up blocked on something controlled by lower-priority threads.

“The problem is that it’s hard to fix a runaway system from within that same system. The tools which you can use to try to fix the system may already have been compromised. And it’s definitely hard to fix a runaway system if your tools have to share critical resources with the thing that is out of control. Windows already gives preferential treatment to the program that is in focus, so if you can get focus onto the taskbar or Task Manager, you are doing about as well as you can. But that preferential treatment takes you only so far if those preferred threads find themselves blocked on things that are controlled by non-preferred threads.”

In the majority of cases, Windows 11 has a workaround for when you want to close a frozen app. For instance, pressing “Ctrl + Alt + Delete” opens a separate screen from which Task Manager can be launched, assuming “Ctrl + Shift + Esc” isn’t working. On Dev Blogs, a developer claims that maxing out all 24 cores of his PC left the Task Manager nearly unusable, and raising its priority helped only slightly, which lines up with Chen’s explanation.

News Source: Microsoft Dev Blogs

item.title: Mario Kart World Already Runs at Full Speed on PC via Switch 2 Emulator Eglantine, Just Over a Week After the Jailbreak
item.description:
Just over a week ago, the Nintendo Switch 2 was finally hacked , roughly sixteen and a half months after its June 2025 debut on the market.

This initial jailbreak opened the gates to the modding, emulation, and homebrew scenes. A few days ago, someone already showed the Switch 2 exclusive game Mario Kart World running on macOS and even on an iPhone 18 Pro ; now, though, the first proper PC emulator has arrived.

Modder Takoroka has released an experimental Switch 2 integration for Eden , one of the first and most famous Switch emulators. The author clearly stated that the software still needs many fixes, but it's a starting point, and others have already used its code to improve it further.

Eglantine builds on Takoroka's experimental Eden NX2 work, offering its own builds of the emerging Switch 2 emulator. The GitHub page says:

Eglantine is a free and open source (FOSS) Switch 2 emulator, derived from Eden, Yuzu, and Sudachi - started by developer Camille LaVey. It's written in C++ with portability in mind, with builds for Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Right now, its makers claim that Mario Kart World is playable at " full speed ", depending on the PC's specs, and the recently released game Splatoon Raiders is also playable, albeit with a variable frame rate. There is video evidence of both on YouTube, as shown in the videos embedded below.

For now, users should view these releases as an experimental starting point that’s still far from a polished way to play the Switch 2's library on PC. Takoroka explicitly warns that missing meshes stem from currently unimplemented shaders. Getting a handful of games running is an encouraging milestone, but broader compatibility, accurate rendering, and consistent performance still have to be achieved.

Still, the speed of progress since the jailbreak is striking and promises much greater results in a short amount of time. On the other hand, this might attract Nintendo's well-known banhammer, which dropped heavily on the Switch emulation scene a couple of years ago, shutting down Yuzu and Ryujinx , two of the most popular emulators.

item.title: ASUS Allegedly Refused To Replace Customer’s $4,480 ROG Strix SCAR 18 Stolen During RMA Shipment, Blames “Insufficient Packaging” After DHL Discarded The Box
item.description:
A customer has accused ASUS Germany of refusing to replace his ludicrously expensive €4,000 (turns out to be nearly $4,500) ROG Strix SCAR 18 that went missing while being shipped in for an official warranty repair. According to the customer, the company is blaming the packaging, even though the only physical evidence was thrown away by the carrier DHL.

Under German and EU law, DHL is ASUS’ contract partner, meaning that the company should honor the warranty

A Reddit post from user “u/No-Goat2559” provides details on the ROG Strix SCAR 18, with the model number G835LX-SA099W, and notes that the gaming laptop was sent to ASUS using a prepaid DHL Germany return label provided directly by the Taiwanese firm. The owner claims that the machine was carefully padded and securely packed. However, on October 9, 2026, DHL’s tracking status reportedly updated to say the damaged shipment had been disposed of because its contents were missing.

The user believes the package was broken into, the laptop was stolen in transit, and DHL then discarded the empty box instead of returning it or delivering it to ASUS. After the customer opened a service case, ASUS’s service back office reportedly investigated and rejected any replacement or refund. The justification was a brief, automated-looking response from DHL claiming the packaging was insufficient.

The customer argues that claim doesn’t hold up, as there are no photos of the packaging and no inspection report, and DHL destroyed the box that could have settled the matter. They also say ASUS forwarded them an internal document marked confidential, which allegedly acknowledges that the gaming laptop manufacturer wasn’t involved in the inspection and has no further proof of its own.

The user’s argument is largely a legal one. They contend that under German and EU law, ASUS ordered and paid for the shipping label, making it DHL’s contract partner and the party that bears the transit risk for warranty returns. In their view, blaming the packaging when the carrier disposed of the evidence without a report results in the spoliation of evidence. So far, the customer hasn’t contested these findings in a court or consumer protection body.

Also, trying to communicate with ASUS via email has been frustrating, as he continues to receive a 550 address rejected error, prompting him to post on Reddit to escalate the matter. A $4,500 bill paid for a premium gaming laptop isn’t a laughing matter, and the user hopes the company honors the warranty and sends him a replacement unit.

It’s worth noting that neither ASUS nor DHL has provided their side of the matter, and carrier liability rules can be a bit complicated. We certainly hope that the matter is resolved swiftly because we’d be fuming too if our expensive machine was stolen in transit.

News Source: Reddit

item.title: NUVIA Co-Founder Gerard Williams Takes A Possible Veiled Jab At Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, Saying “Real Progress Isn’t Just About Pushing Frequencies Higher”
item.description:
Qualcomm's fully custom Oryon cores that debuted with the Snapdragon X Elite and Snapdragon 8 Elite wouldn't have been possible without the NUVIA acquisition, a company co-founded by none other than Gerard Williams. Even though the former Qualcomm and Apple employee is no longer employed at the chipset maker, he hasn't shied away from making remarks about certain SoCs.

In one of his posts, he makes a veiled criticism of the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 , despite not explicitly naming the silicon. However, he does mention that progress isn't defined by how high a chip's clock speed is, and believes that there's an entirely different meaning to CPU architectural design.

The NUVIA co-founder also says that “great CPU architectures deliver more work per clock cycle and per watt”

Williams departed from Qualcomm earlier this year after a four-year tenure, and it's possible that he didn't leave on the best of terms, as his X post is evidence of a strike at his former employer. He argues that the architectural decisions made today determine the performance headroom available tomorrow. He also added that “real progress isn't just about pushing frequencies higher or consuming more power. It's about making the right tradeoffs.”

In a follow-up post, he mentions that "great CPU architectures deliver more work per clock cycle and per watt, while creating room to scale across generations." With the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, not only has Qualcomm adopted TSMC's newest 2nm process, but it's the industry's first smartphone silicon to boast clock speeds of 5.00GHz. Unfortunately, the San Diego firm's lofty ambitions of targeting higher frequencies and power limits have landed it in hot water.

The targeted 5.00GHz frequency has allegedly resulted in the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6's extreme overheating and throttling issues , at least according to Samsung's internal tests, though Qualcomm's Chief Marketing Officer, Don McGuire, has denied these claims . A separate report claimed that the Exynos 2700 is 20 percent faster in CPU and GPU tests than the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, again based on unconfirmed internal tests.

Williams's post doesn't confirm anything about the chip, and it may simply be a general reflection on CPU design. Still, the post was published shortly after Qualcomm faced overheating rumors, a rival's flattering internal numbers, and layoffs . Until commercial devices reach independent reviewers, the claims on both sides should be treated with caution.

item.title: Digital Extremes Puts Soulframe Preludes in Community Hands, as Its Early Alpha Playtest Opens November 6 to All PC Players and Adds Rideable Wolves
item.description:
Today, Digital Extremes announced the imminent opening of its early Alpha playtest of Soulframe Preludes to all PC players. Next week, the Canadian developer is removing the invitation requirement for its in-development fantasy action RPG, so everyone can get in starting Friday, November 6 .

The announcement goes alongside the unveiling of Preludes 17: Verse of the Veilands , a major update introducing rideable wolf mounts and a reworked progression structure built around reclaiming corrupted regions. During a press preview attended by Wccftech, the developers also addressed my question about expanding group activities and making it easier to experience the game cooperatively.

Open Preludes is not Soulframe's finished release, nor does it mark a Steam or console launch. Players will still access the game through its own PC launcher , available from Soulframe's website. The Founders program will remain active, but purchasing access will no longer be necessary to join the ongoing test.

Digital Extremes on Group Activities and Matchmaking

With Soulframe opening to a wider audience, I asked whether Digital Extremes plans to increase its MMO-like elements, particularly group activities, over time. Lead Designer Scott McGregor and Creative Director Geoff Crookes emphasized that cooperative play is fundamental to the game, with matchmaking improvements in development:

Yeah, I think one of the focuses is matchmaking and getting players together. We added the world trees that you could—it was like a hub, so players could discover each other there.

I believe they were working on matchmaking going into dungeons and different Votives as well. I’m not sure if that’s going to make it into this update, but getting players into groups and experiencing the game through co-op is a big, important part of the development of the game. It is a co-op game. It’s designed to be that way.

So making it easier for players to make those groups, even in a public matchmaking sense, is important, definitely will be a focus in either this update or the coming updates, if there’s not some stuff that leaks in. Because there’s stuff always in progress, right? So it could be the following update that we have a bigger push to get players playing it more co-op.

That is a commitment to improving matchmaking , rather than confirmation of raids or a similar category of content dedicated specifically to player groups. The developers also stopped short of guaranteeing that dungeon and Votive matchmaking would arrive in Preludes 17 . However, their answer at least makes clear that bringing players together through public matchmaking is a near-term priority, not just a distant ambition.

Reclaiming the World Gives Players a Clearer Purpose

Verse of the Veilands also changes how players progress through the land of Midrath . Following the Torment Stag encounter, Envoys will begin reclaiming regions affected by Ode'n corruption . Siphons drain energy from the land, leaving areas harsher and disrupting wildlife, resources, and activities. Players complete Votives (the game's missions) and work with local enclave representatives to build energy, learn a region's sacred song, and cleanse its siphon.

Restoration has practical consequences beyond making the landscape more welcoming: wildlife and activities such as fishing and seasonal events return , while healed regions offer different loot and resources. The developers described this as reinforcing the player's role as a healer and giving permanence to their actions in the world.

The Votive system has also been reworked to address feedback from players who enjoyed the opening quests but subsequently struggled to understand what to do next. After meeting the relevant enclave representative, missions can be accepted from the world map, making activities and progression easier to follow. Additional writing and voice acting will give those representatives a more integrated role in the adventure.

Wolf Mounts, a New Pact, and Seasonal Content

Players who have been raising wolf pups will finally be able to mature them into rideable Omen Wolves . Doing so requires progressing through the Veilands to obtain the Barn Biscuit recipe, then preparing it with Verminia. Growing the pup is a choice, rather than an automatic transformation. Other planned additions include Ode Shrike , a hunter/poacher-inspired Pact focused on traps and deception, new weapons and armor, enemy variants, fish, and cave generation updates. The returning seasonal event will also bring new rewards.

Ultimately, the big news of this Soulframe update is that the barrier to participation is going away : anyone on PC can now join the development journey, while the team continues to refine progression, combat, and cooperative play based on player feedback. There's still no ETA on a full release, though, nor any word on console ports.

item.title: BioWare’s Mass Effect Team of Around 50 People Lost Out to Star Wars Battlefront 3 as EA Sidelined Laura Miele, Its Key Advocate
item.description:
EA 's decision to shut down BioWare and cancel the next Mass Effect installment, the ambitious Universe , reportedly came down to a choice between funding its production or another expensive sci-fi project: Star Wars Battlefront 3 , which is being made by DICE and Respawn .

The news comes from Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier , who learned that the publisher chose Star Wars as financial pressure pushed it toward what executives considered the safer bet. In a video accompanying his latest Bloomberg newsletter , Schreier said his reporting draws on conversations with people familiar with strategy at both EA and BioWare. Crucially, Battlefront 3 has not even entered development yet ; it was a prospective project that emerged fairly recently from discussions with Lucasfilm.

Schreier clarifies that the opportunity to make another Battlefront arose several months ago, following renewed interest in Battlefront 2 . At the same time, EA was reviewing its portfolio amid the financial demands of its $55 billion leveraged buyout from a consortium of investors led by PIF. The transaction places approximately $18 billion in debt on EA, with annual interest payments exceeding $1 billion .

Both prospective projects would require hundreds of millions of dollars . Battlefront 3 would need to be built from scratch, while Mass Effect remained in relatively early development with around 50 people at BioWare, and completing the RPG would have required substantially expanding that team or bringing in external development support.

Despite being announced in 2020, Mass Effect Universe was still years away. Schreier attributes much of that delay to its developers spending roughly a year and a half to two years helping finish Dragon Age: The Veilguard , including work on its final mission. So, when push came to shove, EA decided to prioritize Battlefront 3 rather than fund both games. Schreier identifies that investment decision as the largest factor behind BioWare’s closure, although not the only one.

The studio's recent record also weighed against it . The Veilguard missed expectations, Anthem was a major failure, and Mass Effect: Andromeda suffered a mixed critical reception. Schreier argues that EA's executives also understand shooters and predictable franchise releases better than the development demands of sprawling, branching RPGs , and there's ample evidence for that; even Jennifer Hale and Mark Darrah publicly stated that the publisher never really understood what BioWare is all about.

An executive reshuffle reportedly compounded the problem. Laura Miele , described by Schreier as an important advocate for BioWare and Mass Effect , was sidelined, while David Tinson and Cam Weber gained influence. Both have substantial backgrounds in EA's sports business. The result was a round of layoffs that extended well beyond BioWare's remaining staff, with another 350 jobs cut elsewhere in the company. Meanwhile, Amazon's Mass Effect television adaptation is still moving forward, so the franchise's screen ambitions have survived even as its next game has not.

For BioWare fans, the particularly painful detail is that Mass Effect apparently lost out to a game that had not yet started development . Schreier's account tells us of a publisher in financial trouble choosing where to place its next enormous investment, and deciding BioWare's RPG was the riskier proposition. To be honest, Battlefront 3 is easily going to sell a lot more copies than a new Mass Effect would , especially with the degraded trust in the studio's ability to make hits. That explains the decision, but it does nothing to soften the loss of such a historic RPG developer.

Fans are still hoping it will somehow be saved by a third party. In the meantime, the Change.org petition is nearing 285K signatures .

As per a prominent leaker, Intel's upcoming Nova Lake CPUs could deliver up to 20% higher gaming performance than Arrow Lake.

Intel 28-Core Nova Lake Chip Expected to Benefit Significantly From APX, and Could Deliver Substantially Higher Gaming Performance Than Arrow Lake

As we get closer to the launch of Intel's next-generation CPUs , we are getting a glimpse of the performance through leaks. We still don't have the official charts or any benchmarks on popular platforms, but according to recent reports by prominent leakers, it appears that Nova Lake is going to deliver a substantial performance boost over Arrow Lake.

Prominent leaker @Haze2K1 has posted some numbers associated with the Nova Lake-S processors and has claimed that the upcoming chips could deliver up to a good 20% boost in gaming performance vs. Arrow Lake. As per the leaker, Nova Lake could deliver up to 17% higher raw single-threaded performance with bLLC enabled and up to 8% without it. The 20% improvement in gaming performance is reportedly through Intel's Advanced Performance Extensions, or APX, and somewhat coincides with the August leak.

APEX is an x86 instruction set extension that is designed to improve CPU execution efficiency. The most notable change here is the doubling of the number of general-purpose registers from 16 to 32 in 64-bit mode. Due to more registers, the need to move data between registers and memory is reduced, which, as a result, causes fewer unnecessary memory accesses. Games could therefore benefit from these changes, although the actual gains will depend on software optimizations and compiler support.

According to the leaker, the APX could contribute about 15% higher performance, and from August's leak, we learned that the 28-core configurations could deliver a solid 16% higher gaming performance vs. Core Ultra 9 285K when the CPU operates at 285W PL1. At 296W PL1 , the gaming performance supposedly sees a 33% boost , which is a significant change, but Nova Lake is also going to feature 8000 MT/s DDR5 support out of the box, which should be a major factor in higher performance.

Intel needs this if it really wants to compete against AMD's X3D processors, which have been dominating the gaming workloads for a while now. Arrow Lake didn't bring any noticeable gaming benefits over Raptor Lake Refresh, but if Intel can manage to bring 20-30% higher gaming performance with Nova Lake, it could shake AMD's CPU share in the mainstream market.

At the same time, it's equally important to price the products right. A 28-core bLLC variant will likely end up in the premium segment, but if Intel prices it aggressively, as it does with the Arrow Lake Refresh, Nova Lake can be a true competitor to AMD's X3D chips.

item.title: 4KW AC Radiator Got Tested On An RTX 3080 By YouTuber, Overkill Cooler Drops GPU Temperatures By Nearly 40°C And Pushes Its Power Limit To 450W+
item.description:
A YouTuber pulled out a 4kW AC radiator to test out multiple NVIDIA GPUs, including the RTX 3080, to see just how well this cooling solution would perform. As an added bonus, the content creator also added the notoriously power-hungry and prone-to-fail Core i9-14900K to see if the same cooler could handle both components running in unison. The results show that this setup worked better than expected.

The AC radiator was also tested on the RTX 5060, but its lack of overclocking headroom didn't make it a practical experiment

By creating a proper water loop, as enthusiasts do for their custom builds, the YouTube channel TrashBench repurposed a used Fujitsu AC radiator into a CPU and GPU cooler. With a few modifications here and there, the first candidate was the RTX 5060. Unfortunately, due to the lack of overclocking headroom, there was little purpose in attaching such a monster of a cooler to a graphics card that wouldn't benefit from this cooling, so an RTX 3080 was used in its place.

As you can see, at stock clock speeds, the RTX 3080's GPU temperatures dropped by 37°C, which obviously meant that there is a ton of flexibility when overclocking the graphics card, especially when there is insane cooling at TrashBench's disposal. With its stock power limit in the 320W-350W range, the AC radiator helped raise that figure to 459W, with its core clock increased to 2,130MHz. To really push the limits of this configuration, Intel's notorious Core i9-14900K was added to the mix.

When running a combined CPU and GPU test, the Core i9-14900K reached a 230W power limit, but its temperature only dropped from 74.8°C to 71.7°C. TrashBench notes that such a miniature delta was likely due to using an unspecified water block, which may not have provided proper contact with the processor, leading to underwhelming results. Regardless, the YouTuber states that he is surprised at how well the AC radiator worked, but the stock pump used was incredibly noisy.

Then again, if an AIO tailor-made for CPUs and GPUs can produce such incredible thermal results, it is no surprise that an AC radiator should perform miles ahead.

item.title: AI Boom Triggers Massive PCB Shortage With Orders Booked Until 2030, Posing Big Challenges For Consumer Hardware Vendors
item.description:
Not just memory and NAND, but PCB costs are apparently rising rapidly as well, thanks to the AI boom.

AI Infrastructure Demand is Reportedly Gobbling up the PCB Supply, Which Could Make Consumer Hardware Even More Expensive

Not just memory, SSDs, and GPUs are surging in costs , but the PCBs (printed circuit boards) are about to see a significant surge in prices in the near future. The AI boom has spared nothing, and that's exactly what the latest report by Nikkei Asia suggests. According to the report, many manufacturers are now struggling to secure enough capacity to meet the demand from both AI and traditional electronics markets.

Nikkei Asia reports that PCB manufacturers are seeing order lead times stretch to as long as 30 months. This is why one supplier told the outlet that the orders placed today may not be fulfilled until late 2028. An unnamed executive from an American PC vendor revealed that securing sufficient PCB supplies is becoming increasingly difficult, despite expectations of declining PC shipments next year.

Even though PC shipments could decline again next year, we are still struggling to secure enough PCB supplies to meet our needs

This is a result of PCB supplies being gobbled up by the AI infrastructure, which is rapidly expanding and is attracting significantly more investment and manufacturing capacity than consumer electronics. PCB manufacturers are naturally prioritizing orders from customers who are willing to pay more, which is leaving conventional PC vendors competing for the remaining production capacity.

That said, the problem isn't just the limited PCB manufacturing capacity. The report suggests that the materials required to create these boards are also becoming significantly more expensive. Copper-clad laminates or CCLs that is an essential part of PCB construction, have witnessed price hikes a dozen times since July, 2026. So, simply expanding the manufacturing capacities might not resolve the supply crunch anytime soon.

For the consumer segment, this can be a headache for vendors as maintaining a steady supply of components at lower prices is already challenging, and now with increased PCB costs and limited availability, the overall production costs will see a drastic rise.

News Sources: Nikkei Asia , Tom's Hardware

item.title: PlayStation 6 and Xbox Project Helix Are Set to Cost $1000 or More, but Sony’s Cloud Gaming Patent Could Make Streaming a Reliable Entry Point
item.description:
With hardware prices spiking in the past few months and no signs of the situation improving, the PlayStation 6 and Xbox Project Helix are set to cost significantly more than their predecessors, prompting more than a few gamers to consider alternatives to enjoy upcoming games. While cloud gaming has become a viable alternative, it only delivers a good experience with a good internet connection, but Sony may have solved this issue with new technology that uses AI to improve quality in a rather clever way.

"Techniques for reducing data content in an image, including receiving an image at a first data model, removing a plurality of image portions from the image, using a machine learning inference process implemented by the first data model, to thereby insert a plurality of holes in the image and inserting, using the machine learning inference process implemented, at least one anchor element into one or more of the plurality of holes, wherein each anchor element is representative of detail within the respective image portion," reads the overview of the patent by Sony published on October 29 , as reported by Patentlyze .

In simpler terms, this patent outlines a technology that uses an AI model to punch a literal hole in a streamed video game scene and have another model rebuild it later, potentially eliminating issues deriving from a low-quality internet connection, including latency.

Going more in depth, this new technology utilizes first a decimation network running on the sender's side. This network takes the image being sent to play, divides it into a grid with a score for each part, and uses these scores to determine which parts can be cut (those below a 0.4 score). A reconstruction network runs on the receiving device, filling the gaps without the player noticing. This technology is also quite versatile, as the network can be assigned a target image quality or compression level as input, which determines how many holes the decimation network bores into the image and how many are reconstructed on the receiving end.

Needless to say, this PlayStation technology could work wonders for cloud gaming as a whole, as the less data is sent over an internet connection, the more responsive the experience will be. On the other hand, there could be significant issues if the reconstruction network doesn't work as intended, as AI could invent details that were never there in the original game scene.

Regardless of its caveats, this new PlayStation technology sounds as promising as others that leverage AI to improve gameplay , and could power a new affordable entry point into next-generation gaming, and potentially even improve the Remote Play experience on the PlayStation Portal , which has proven to be even more popular than Sony anticipated . For certain genres such as competitive shooters or fighting games where every frame matters, this technology will change little, but for single-player experiences that don't require instant reactions, I can definitely see it working in some capacity.

item.title: Corsair HS80 v2 MAX Wireless Review: Corsair’s Most Comfortable Gaming Headset Gets a Worthy Evolution, Not a Reinvention
item.description:
Product Info
Corsair HS80 v2 MAX
October 2026
Type
Wireless headset
Price
$199.99

Introduction

Few gaming headsets have left as positive an impression on me as the original Corsair HS80 RGB Wireless. When I reviewed it back in 2021, I praised its excellent comfort, strong audio performance, and impressive microphone quality. Over the years, Corsair has expanded its headset portfolio considerably, with products such as the HS75 XB Wireless , Virtuoso XT, Virtuoso Max , Void Wireless V2 , and HS35 v3 Wireless all targeting different segments of the market.

The HS80 v2 MAX arrives as the latest evolution of that formula. Rather than reinventing the HS80, Corsair has focused on refining an already successful headset by improving battery life, expanding connectivity options, updating the microphone, and introducing a new driver design. After spending time with the headset across PC, PlayStation 5, and mobile devices, it quickly became clear that the HS80 v2 MAX remains true to the series' gaming-first philosophy. More importantly, it addresses several of the shortcomings of previous HS80 models without sacrificing the strengths that made the original so easy to recommend.

Design and Build Quality

At first glance, it would be easy to mistake the HS80 v2 MAX for the original HS80 RGB Wireless. Corsair has made only subtle changes to the overall design, and frankly, I think that was the right decision. The headset retains the familiar floating suspension headband, aluminum frame, RGB logos, and fabric-covered memory foam ear cushions. While some may have been hoping for a complete redesign, the original HS80 remains one of the better-looking gaming headsets on the market. It avoids excessive gamer aesthetics while still looking modern and premium.

Build quality is excellent throughout. The aluminum yokes inspire confidence, the earcups feel solid, and there are no obvious weak points in the construction. Having previously used both the Virtuoso XT and Virtuoso Max, I would still place those models slightly ahead in terms of perceived luxury, but the HS80 v2 MAX feels every bit as well built as I'd expect from a headset in this price range.

Comfort

Comfort was arguably the biggest strength of the original HS80, and it remains one of the biggest reasons to consider the HS80 v2 MAX. The floating suspension headband remains one of my favourite aspects of the HS80 design. Rather than creating pressure points on top of the head, the self-adjusting strap distributes weight remarkably evenly across the head, making the headset extremely comfortable during longer gaming sessions. This is something rival brand SteelSeries has been doing successfully for years with its Arctis lineup, and Corsair's implementation works every bit as well.

Despite weighing more than some competing headsets, the HS80 v2 MAX never felt particularly heavy during use. I regularly wore the headset for several hours while gaming and listening to music without experiencing any significant discomfort. The fabric-covered ear cushions are another highlight. While leatherette pads may offer slightly better isolation, I continue to prefer fabric pads for extended use. They remain cooler, especially during longer gaming sessions, and contribute significantly to the headset's overall comfort. In this regard, Corsair has wisely avoided fixing something that wasn't broken.

Connectivity

Connectivity is one of the HS80 v2 MAX's biggest strengths, but also one of its few weaknesses. The addition of simultaneous Bluetooth and Slipstream Wireless connectivity is a welcome upgrade over previous HS80 models and places the headset more in line with what buyers increasingly expect from a premium wireless gaming headset. During testing, being connected to both a gaming platform and a smartphone simultaneously proved genuinely useful for Discord, phone calls and music playback.

Compatibility extends to PC, Mac, PlayStation, Nintendo Switch and mobile devices, covering the vast majority of gaming platforms. The notable omission is Xbox support. While Corsair is certainly not alone in this regard, the limitation becomes more apparent given the HS80 v2 MAX's $199.99 price point. Several competing headsets in this segment, including SteelSeries' Arctis Nova 7X and Turtle Beach's Stealth 700 series, offer broader console compatibility while also supporting PC and mobile devices. As a result, gamers invested in both the Xbox and PlayStation ecosystems may find those alternatives slightly more appealing.

For PC and PlayStation gamers this will likely be irrelevant. However, gamers who regularly switch between Xbox and PlayStation may find greater value in alternatives that support both platforms from a single headset. As a result, the HS80 v2 MAX falls slightly short of being the ultimate multiplatform solution.

Battery Life

Battery life is easily one of the most impressive aspects of the HS80 v2 MAX. The original HS80 never had poor battery life, but it certainly couldn't compete with many modern wireless headsets. Corsair has clearly recognized that limitation and made battery endurance a major priority this time around.

Throughout my testing, battery anxiety simply wasn't a concern. In fact, battery life proved to be one of the most significant upgrades over the original HS80 RGB Wireless. Whereas charging the older model occasionally became part of my routine, the HS80 v2 MAX often went several days before I even considered reaching for the charging cable. While actual runtime naturally varies depending on volume levels, RGB settings, and connection methods, I consistently found battery life to be substantially better than every previous HS80 model I've used. This is particularly impressive given the addition of simultaneous Bluetooth and Slipstream Wireless connectivity, a feature that can negatively impact endurance on some competing headsets. The inclusion of fast charging is equally welcome. Even after forgetting to charge the headset, a quick top-up provided enough battery to comfortably get through an evening of gaming. For many users, battery life alone may be reason enough to upgrade from an older HS80.

Microphone Quality

Corsair has built a reputation for delivering some of the best microphones in the gaming headset market, and the HS80 v2 MAX continues that tradition. Voice recordings sounded clear, natural, and detailed, with noticeably better clarity than many competing wireless gaming headsets. Teammates consistently reported that my voice sounded clean and easy to understand during multiplayer sessions. The integrated flip-to-mute design remains extremely convenient, while NVIDIA Broadcast integration provides additional options for users looking to reduce background noise. While dedicated USB microphones still have an obvious advantage, the HS80 v2 MAX delivers one of the strongest microphone performances I've encountered in a wireless gaming headset.

Software

Like most Corsair peripherals, the HS80 v2 MAX integrates with iCUE. The software provides extensive control over EQ presets, RGB lighting, microphone settings, Dolby Atmos features, and NVIDIA Broadcast functionality. Users already invested in Corsair's ecosystem will appreciate the level of customization available. That said, my opinion on iCUE remains largely unchanged. It is powerful, but also more complex than it really needs to be. Fortunately, most settings can be configured once and largely forgotten.

Audio Performance

Gaming

Gaming is clearly where the HS80 v2 MAX feels most at home. Corsair's new 50mm NNL drivers appear to have been designed specifically with gaming performance in mind, and the results are impressive. Positional cues remain easy to identify, directional information is precise, and the headset does an excellent job separating important sounds from the overall mix. In competitive shooters, footsteps and environmental cues were easy to pick out, even during more chaotic firefights. Explosions retain plenty of impact without overwhelming the rest of the soundscape, while dialogue remains clean and intelligible. Dolby Atmos support further enhances immersion in supported titles, creating a convincing sense of spatial awareness and helping the headset maintain its competitive gaming credentials.

Simply put, the HS80 v2 MAX sounds exactly like a headset designed by people who understand gaming.

Music

Music performance is very good, although the headset remains unmistakably gaming-focused. Bass is punchy and energetic without becoming completely dominant. Modern pop, electronic music, and movie soundtracks benefit from the additional low-end presence, while vocals remain clear and well positioned within the mix.

Compared to the Virtuoso Max, the HS80 v2 MAX sounds slightly less refined and offers somewhat less detail retrieval. The Virtuoso remains Corsair's stronger all-round multimedia headset. However, the gap is smaller than I expected, and for casual music listening, the HS80 v2 MAX performs admirably.

Movies and Media

The headset is equally enjoyable for movies, streaming content, and general media consumption. The combination of strong bass performance, comfortable fit, long battery life, and Dolby Atmos support makes it particularly well-suited for lengthy viewing sessions. Dialogue reproduction is excellent, while action scenes benefit from the headset's energetic presentation. The ability to remain connected to both a mobile device and gaming platform simultaneously further increases its versatility as an everyday headset.

Closing thoughts

The HS80 v2 MAX is not a revolutionary upgrade over the original HS80 RGB Wireless, but it doesn't need to be. Corsair has focused on meaningful improvements where they matter most, addressing nearly every weakness of its predecessor while preserving the comfort and gaming-first design philosophy that made the original headset such a success. Battery life is dramatically improved, simultaneous Bluetooth and Slipstream Wireless connectivity adds genuine day-to-day versatility, and the upgraded microphone remains among the strongest available in a wireless gaming headset. Combined with excellent comfort and strong gaming performance, the HS80 v2 MAX feels like the most complete HS80 headset Corsair has produced to date.

However, the headset's connectivity story is not entirely perfect. While support for PC, Mac, PlayStation, Nintendo Switch, and mobile devices is comprehensive, the absence of Xbox compatibility becomes more noticeable at the $199.99 price point. Competing headsets in this segment often offer broader ecosystem support, making them a potentially better fit for gamers who regularly switch between Xbox and PlayStation consoles. For PC and PlayStation gamers, this limitation is unlikely to matter. In fact, the HS80 v2 MAX remains one of the most compelling wireless gaming headsets currently available thanks to its comfort, battery life, microphone performance, and dual-wireless connectivity. Multiplaform gamers invested in both Xbox and PlayStation ecosystems may want to explore alternatives, but everyone else will find a highly capable headset that successfully improves upon an already excellent predecessor.
